analytic.title: UCaS: A Schedulability Analysis Tool for AADL Models

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: There is more and more the ubiquitous use of different types of real-time embedded (RTE) systems in our daily lives with rapid developments in science and technology. Because design faults might result in injury or even death to human beings who are using these systems, how to ensure the RTE systems are really safe is very important. The schedulability problem is a very important problem needs to be guaranteed in real-time software. In this paper, based on the Architecture Analysis and Design Language (AADL), we present Hybrid Automaton with Relative Time Constraints (HARTC) and Arrival Time Automaton (ATA) to abstract the semantics and external environment of each thread component in AADL respectively. Thus, we translate the schedulability problem in the system modeled by AADL into the reachability problem of locations in the product of HARTCs and ATAs. Then, we study the condition under which the reachability of HARTC is decidable. Under this condition, we develop a schedulability analysis tool called UCaS as a plug-in which can be integrated in the open source tool OSATE. We illustrate the schedulability analysis and simulation result provided by UCaS through an example. Finally, we give future directions need to be solved and our conclusion.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Embedded system is a kind of particular computation systems designed for executing real-time computation and embedded in other physical systems usually. Embedded systems are applied by people in so many safety-critical domains, including avionics, automotive electronics, or robotics systems which all need timing requirements, fault and error behaviors, time and space partitioning, and safety and certification properties. Thus, how to ensure the high safety and security of the RTE software within strict requirements is a big problem.

To solve this, the Society of Automotive Engineers and Avionics Systems Division present an aerospace standard named AADL [1] which was approved in November 2004. It is a textual and graphical language to design and analyze the software and hardware architectures of performance-critical real-time systems. It can describe functional interfaces of components (such as data inputs and outputs) and performancecritical aspects of components (such as execution time and deadline). The AADL can also describe how components interact, such as how data inputs and outputs are connected or how application software components are allocated to execution platform components. From this perspective, the designer can evaluate architectural tradeoffs and changes of RTE systems. In this paper, we assume the readers have had some knowledge about AADL.

After modeling, a necessary work we need to do is to analyze the non-functional properties and simulate the functional behaviors of the system. But, unfortunately, there are a few tools which could only do inadequate schedulability analysis for AADL models. For example, Furness toolset, which could be integrated in OSATE, is a primary tool for simulating AADL models. But its schedulability analysis could not give us the analysis result when aperiodic threads and sporadic threads in the system are dispatched directly by events from the external environment. The details are introduced in our previous work [11].

In conclusion, our paper's contributions include the following: 1) For describing the semantics of systems and their external evironments exactly, we present Hybrid Automaton with Relative Time Constraints (HARTC) and Arrival Time Automaton (ATA) to abstract the semantics of each thread component and its external environment respectively. Then, we translate the schedulability problem in AADL models into reachability problem of the locations in the product of HARTCs and ATAs. 2) We also give the condition under which the reachability problem is decidable. We develop a schedulability analysis tool named UCaS under this decidable condition. This paper is organized as follows: in section 2, we give the detailed definition of the HARTC and ATA. In Section 3, we give an overview of UCaS and an example to illustrate how to use it. We give future research directions and related work in section 4 and conclude in section 5.

div.head: System models
div.p: AADL language could describe the architectures of the real-time reactive systems, which are open and interacting with the environment all the time. In this paper, we just consider the software components in AADL and omit the effect brought by the hardware components in AADL. Thus, we use a novel notation Hybrid Automata with Relative Time Constraints to abstract the system, and use a variational timed automaton named Arrival Time Automaton to denote the external environment of that system. The communication channels between them are synchronous events.

div.head: Internal models
div.p: In AADL, threads are units of execution. Each thread has an associated semantic automaton that describes thread states and conditions on transitions between thread states. For consisting with the semantics of threads when analyzing their schedulability, we present the hybrid automata with relative time constraints which extend singular automata [2] with synchronous events labeled on transitions and some constraints on the variables. We first give the definition of Hybrid Automaton with Relative Time Constraints. Definition 1. (Hybrid Automaton with Relative Time Constraints, HARTC) A hybrid automaton with relative time constraints is a 10-tuple < Sync, L, X, E, init, inv, flow, pre, post, jump>, where Sync is a finite set of synchronous events; L is a finite set of locations; X is a finite set of variables: ∃X init(l)≠ ∅ ∧init(l) x = init(l) y .

In Definition 1, we call the set X 1 clock variables and X 2 stopwatch variables. In the context, unless distinguish them explicitely, we use variable to represent any of them. And we represent the values of variables as functions from X to the non-negative reals 0 ≥ . A variable interpretation ν for a set X of variables assigns a real value to each variable. For t∈ 0 ≥ , ν+t denotes the variable interpretation which maps every variable x to the value ν(x)+t, and the variable interpretation t•ν assigns to each variable x the value t•ν(x). For Y⊆X, [Y t]ν denotes the variable interpretation for X which assigns t to each x∈Y, and agrees with ν over the rest of the variables. According to Definition 1, at any time instant, ν(x) is larger than or at least equals to ν(y) which satisfies <x, y>∈R. Thus, there is a difference between the values of variable x and y in a HARTC for ever and they preserve the standard region equivalence [3].

div.head: External models
div.p: Each thread needs to communicate with its external environment. Thus, we define the external environments by Arrival Time Automata. Each ATA defines the behaviors of external environment of corresponding thread. Then, the product of all the ATAs defines the behaviors of external environment of the whole thread group, i.e. the environment of the system. The way to get the product of ATAs is the same as the way to get the product of the ordinary timed automata [4].

div.head: Schedulability analysis by UCaS
div.p: UCaS is a schedulability analysis tool developed by the group of University of Electronic Science and Technology of China as a plug-in integrated in OSATE.

There are two main parts in UCaS. One is to describe ATAs, i.e. environment of each thread; the other is schedulability analysis engine, illustrated in Figure 3. To describe ATAs, users could input the time instances or time intervals of each synchronous event corresponding to each non-periodic thread. For each periodic thread, UCaS could generate its ATA directly according to the Period property imported from AADL code. After inputing the time instances or intervals of synchronous events, UCaS will do some examination about the time restrictions of sporadic threads, that is, the possible time lengths between several consecutive time instances should not be less than its period value. If all the conditions are right, UCaS will compute the time zone of HARTCs||ATAs in the form of DBM (Difference Bounded Matrix) [5]. If a location of HARTCs||ATAs containing Error i can be reached at some time, UCaS will return the result "nonschedulable" to the users, otherwise, UCaS will return the result "schedulable" to the users.

UCaS can also analyze the systems involved with modes. Mode is a quite useful element in AADL. We need to set Synchronized_component property of each periodic thread in the system true, then the execution of periodic threads will not be interrupted by mode transition and the time of mode transition will be delayed until their hyperperiod time instant. And there is only one mode existed simultaneously: the current mode. Thus, for schedulable analysis, UCaS could only analyze the elements in each mode. If the threads in each mode are all schedulable, then UCaS will return the result "schedulable" to users.

In an AADL project, there may be a fixed number of processors running a fixed number of threads, according to a certain scheduling strategy. Thus, each processor component that has some threads bound to it must have the Scheduling_Protocol property specified. Then, UCaS will analyze the threads in each processor respectively 1 and get the result for each processor respectively. Let us use an example to illustrate how to use UCaS. div.head: Related work and future direction
div.p: Scheduling is a well-established area. Various analysis methods have been published in the literature. Architecture Analysis and Design Language (AADL) is an SAE standard specifically designed to model runtime architectures and analyze their key runtime properties. It precisely defines execution semantics for its components [17,18]. When these methods are applied in an AADL project which may involve nonperiodic threads, they can not make a precise schedulability analysis. The traditional and standard way is to consider non-periodic threads as periodic ones using the estimated minimal inter-arrival times as thread periods. Clearly, the analysis result is pessimistic and imprecise. Timed automata [3] have been used to solve non-preemptive scheduling problems mainly for job-shop scheduling [6]. These techniques specify pre-defined locations of an automaton as goals to achieve by scheduling and use reachability analysis to construct traces leading to the goal locations. And there are several work [7,8] using stop-watch automata to model preemptive scheduling problems. But the reachability problem of stop-watch automata is undecidable in general [9]. TIMES [10] identified a decidable class of updatable automata, i.e. the timed automata extended with tasks to analyze schedulability. But unfortunately, the aperiodic tasks in TIMES have different semantics as them in AADL. That's because AADL defines an event queue on each event port of each thread. If it has been dispatched (not finished yet), and some events come to its event ports, these events should be waiting until the thread finished and then dispatch it again, an event will be moved from that queue at the same time. That is, for each aperiodic thread in AADL, there must be at most one instance at any time. But, in TIMES, there is no port in any task, that means if an event triggers a task, then another instanace of it will be create immediately. Thus, for each aperiodic task in TIMES, there may exist several instances simultaneously. Clearly, the former is much complex than the latter. But, we can still use TIMES to analyze and simulate the threads in AADL without aperiodic threads [11].

For schedulability analysis of AADL, there are some methods could analyze a subset of it. MetaH [12], a precursor to AADL, offers schedulability analysis for rate-monotonic priority assignments. Literature [13] converts a small subset of AADL elements into process algebra ACSR to do schedulability analysis. The current version of UCaS could not analyze the systems involved with delayed connections and the hardware components. Thus, one of the future directions for us is to solve these shortcomings and make a more precise schedulability result for an AADL project. Another future direction for us is to analyze the schedulability of systems which are involved with error models defined in AADL Error Model Annex [15]. Ana Rugina presented a way to generate generalized stochastic petri nets from error models for evaluating dependability measures [16]. We need to consider the abstraction of error models in the form of automata, thus, we can analyze the schedulability and dependability in a uniform semantics instead of analyzing them respectively in different semantics.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: A key concern of our work of this paper is to present Hybrid Automata with Relative Time Constraints, an extended version of singular automata with synchronous events labeled on transitions and some constraints on the variables for abstracting the semantics of thread components in AADL in the design cycle statically. In addition, we present Arrival Time Automaton to model the external environment of each thread component. And then, we discuss the condition under which the reachability problem of locations in the product of HARTCs and ATAs is decidable. This is a decidability result for scheduling analysis in dense time models also, besides the task automata [14]. Thus, according to this condition, we develop a schedulability analysis tool named UCaS. It could get an intuitive conclusion whether the threads are schedulable or not, and could show the simulation trace also. At last, we give an example to illustrate the convenience of UCaS.
